cards.prompt: Imagine a small model that has only read space adventure stories, full of lines like "Captain Rivera stepped onto Mars". It gets this text. Which word is it **most likely** to write next?
cards.context: The first person to walk on Mars was
cards.hint: It isn't choosing what's true. What did this model read again and again?
cards.nudge: Think about the stories this model learned from. Which word filled this spot in them?
cards.explanation: Nobody has walked on Mars yet, and Neil Armstrong walked on the **Moon**. But in this model's stories, sentences like this carry on with "**Captain** …", so it's likely to invent a Mars walker, one likely word at a time. (Big chatbots have seen this question and usually get it right; the risk is highest for things they've seen less.)

cards.title: Fluent, confident, wrong
cards.body: A **hallucination** is when a chatbot says something false, smoothly and confidently. It picks words that *sound* likely, not facts it has checked, so a made-up book sounds as real as a true one. Watch names, dates, numbers, quotes and sources. Check them in a trusted source, like a library catalogue. Asking the chatbot "are you sure?" checks nothing.

cards.prompt: You're writing a report on volcanoes.

steps.text: A chatbot suggests the book "Fire Below" by Dr Helen Marsh, with a confident summary and a quote for your report. What do you do?

choices.text: Use the quote: it's from a book
choices.consequence: Nobody can find the book anywhere, because it doesn't exist. A made-up quote in a report is a real problem.

choices.text: Search for the book in the library catalogue
choices.consequence: No results, for the book or the author. A great title, a confident author, and one small problem: none of it exists.

choices.text: Ask the chatbot if the book is real
choices.consequence: It says "Yes, it's a well-known book!" It can be just as confident about a hallucination.

steps.text: The library has never heard of it. What now?

choices.text: Leave it out, and find a real source in the library
choices.consequence: Right: the book was a hallucination. A real source gives you facts you can trust, and quote.

choices.text: Keep the quote, but don't say where it's from
choices.consequence: The quote is made up too, so it's still not true, and now it's hidden. Use a real source.

cards.hint: What's a trusted source for whether a book exists?
cards.explanation: Book titles, authors and quotes are classic hallucinations. **Check them in a trusted source**, like a library catalogue. Asking the chatbot doesn't help: it can be confidently wrong about its own mistakes.

cards.prompt: Would you **double-check** each thing a chatbot gives you, or is it **fine to use** as it is? (Anything about health always goes to a doctor, a pharmacist or a trusted adult.)

items.label: A date for a history project
A quote from a famous scientist
A website it says it got facts from
Names for a new team group chat

cards.hint: Ask: if it were made up, would it matter? Names, dates, quotes and sources are where hallucinations hide.
cards.nudge: Ideas can't really be wrong. Facts, quotes, sources and anything about health can be, and it matters.
cards.explanation: Dates, quotes, sources and anything about health are **facts** that could be hallucinated, and getting them wrong matters, so double-check. Medicine questions go to a doctor, a pharmacist or a trusted adult. Party themes, rhymes and chat names are fine: there's no "wrong" to catch.

cards.prompt: A chatbot tells you a fact you need for a report at work. What's the **best** way to check it?

options.text: Find it in a trusted source, like a textbook or an official website
Ask the same question again and see if the two answers match
options.nudge: A chatbot can repeat the same mistake. Where can you check it outside the chatbot?

options.text: Ask the chatbot to explain how it knows, and if it's sure
options.nudge: It can be confidently wrong about its own mistakes. Where else could you look?

options.text: Ask a different chatbot and see if it gives the same answer
options.nudge: Another chatbot can make the same kind of mistake. Where can you check outside chatbots?

cards.hint: The check has to come from somewhere that isn't a chatbot.
cards.explanation: Only a **trusted source** outside chatbots really checks a fact. Asking again, asking it how it knows, or asking a different chatbot all stay inside chatbots, which can repeat or defend a hallucination.

cards.prompt: A chatbot tells you a famous ship sank in **1915**, and gives a link to a museum website.

steps.text: You click the link, and it opens a real museum page about the ship. What now?

choices.text: Use 1915: the link works, so it's checked
choices.consequence: The page is real, but you didn't read it. It actually says the ship sank in **1912**. A real link isn't proof of the claim.

choices.text: Read the page and find the date it gives
Ask the chatbot to double-check its date
choices.consequence: It apologises and says 1914. Still not checked: the answer is on the page you already have.

steps.text: The museum page says 1912. The chatbot said 1915. Which do you use?

choices.consequence: Right: the trusted source you actually read wins.

choices.text: 1915: the chatbot found the page, so it knows
choices.consequence: The chatbot linked the right page but wrote the wrong date. Go with what the source really says.

cards.hint: Chatbots can invent sources, or link a real one and get it wrong. A source only checks a fact if it really says what the chatbot claims.
cards.explanation: A link that works isn't enough: chatbots can link a real page and still get the detail wrong. **Read the source**, and go with what it actually says.

cards.prompt: Match each thing a chatbot gives you to what to do about it.

pairs.left: Says where a fact came from
pairs.right: Open the source and read it

cards.hint: For each one, ask: is it a fact to check, a source to open, a health question, or just ideas?
cards.nudge: Ideas can't really be wrong, and health questions need an expert. Which of the other two is about a book, and which about a source?
cards.explanation: Books get checked in a **catalogue**; sources get **opened and read**; medicine questions go to a **doctor or pharmacist**; and party themes are ideas, so there's nothing to catch.

cards.title: Recap
cards.body:
- A **hallucination** is a confident, false answer built from likely words.
- They hide in names, dates, numbers, quotes and sources.
- Check what matters in a trusted source, not by asking again.

Next: the module quiz.
